body: Root cause: PR #912 (AISDLC-538) failed the CI attestation gate because subject.sha1 pointed at an orphaned pre-rebase commit unreachable in CI's shallow clone; the AISDLC-448 tree-equivalence relaxation works locally (orphan in object store) but not CI -> local-passes/CI-fails. Security note: an envelope signed for diff-X's patch-id cannot validate diff-Y (different patch-id -> different filename -> not found); cross-PR reuse requires byte-identical diffs (benign). rationale: Operator decision 2026-06-13: relax. patch-id (envelope filename, from diff content) already content-binds the envelope; Merkle root + trusted-key signature authenticate reviewer evidence; subject.sha1 commit-binding is redundant and the sole source of the orphan-after-rebase CI fragility (4 recovery re-signs in the 2026-06-12 drain, incl PR #912). In-toto/SLSA/Sigstore bind to content digests not commit SHAs. Replay counter-argument answered: cross-PR reuse needs a byte-identical diff = same patch-id = same review (benign). Impl: verifier accepts when content-patch-id==filename + Merkle verifies + trusted signature, WITHOUT subject.sha1 reachability. AISDLC-673 (local head 6dafd29f7, 126 tests passing) has only the test re-review, rebase and sign left. Its owner, executor delta, is unavailable until 2026-10-06. 673 gates 672, 675 and 676, which is the RFC-0052 staged-review critical path. operator-dispatch asked the planner whether alpha or gamma may take it over from delta's worktree.

## Prior art / research
- RFC-0051 §authority matrix: the dispatch tier owns throughput; a durable assignment channel exists so assignments survive an executor being gone.
- RFC-0042/0046: the remaining steps are mechanical; the one trust-sensitive step (reviewer verdicts) must be produced by a fresh reviewer spawn, never copied from another session.
- Earlier same-night call: 681 was NOT handed over, because it was mid-push (a half-pushed branch is not a clean handover point). That call was specific, not a rule.

Pro: critical path keeps moving tonight; no trust shortcut. Con: a second executor spends ~1 task-slot on work it did not author.

- **opt-c: dispatch re-does 673 from scratch in a new worktree.** Pro: no shared-worktree ambiguity. Con: throws away 126 passing tests and a day of work; strictly worse than opt-a.

If 673's committed head has unresolved review findings the handover executor cannot see, it may ship something delta intended to rework. Mitigation: the fresh reviewer spawn is exactly the check that catches that.

body:
## Problem
alpha's 656.1 branch (signed locally, head 5b1f6ec3, based on aeb22661, not pushed) already threads repoId through replay-run.ts, replay-commands.ts and replay-report.ts. Task 653.2 (replay-run records carry repoId; dep 653.1 merged; must precede 656.2) has scope items 1-3 in the same files. Whichever lands second conflicts and may be partly redundant. 653.2 is unclaimed (DoR not done).

## Prior art
- Standing rule: signed, review-complete work is not re-reviewed for ordering reasons alone; a patch-id change forces a fresh review round (RFC-0042 patch-scoped verifier).
- One task per PR; scope trimming of an unclaimed task against already-landed work is a mechanical DoR step, not a design change.

## Options
- **opt-a (recommended):** 656.1 pushes now as is. 653.2 rebases on it when claimed and trims scope to what 656.1 did not cover; if nothing remains of items 1-3, the task body records "items 1-3 landed in 656.1" and keeps only the rest. Pro: zero cost tonight, no re-review, preserves 653.2 as the audit point for 656.2's dependency. Con: 653.2's DoR must verify the overlap honestly.
- **opt-b:** 653.2 first, then 656.1 rebases and re-reviews. Pro: tasks land in numeric dependency order. Con: throws away a signed review on finished work for an ordering that nothing depends on.
- **opt-c:** fold 653.2 items 1-3 into 656.1 and mark 653.2 reduced/done. Pro: fewest PRs. Con: changes 656.1's reviewed scope after sign (re-review anyway), and 656.2's dependency on 653.2 then points at a task that was partly closed by a different PR; muddier audit trail.

## Counter-argument
If 653.2's items 1-3 differ semantically from what 656.1 did (for example a different repoId source), trimming hides a real design difference. Mitigation: the 653.2 DoR compares item by item against 656.1's diff before trimming; any divergence becomes a question back to the planner.
by: planner (Claude Fable 5.1, on behalf of dominique@reliablegenius.io)

rationale: Recommended option taken: finished, signed work ships; the unclaimed task absorbs the rebase and scope-trim at its DoR step. Operator may override via cli-decisions override.

## Problem
Gamma's rebased 673 head 8dba37eb is approved by all three reviewers (no critical/major) but carries two security MEDIUMs: (1) compare-probe revisions are only syntax-checked, so a plan can name any local ref (including the shared stash, which can hold untracked .env) and diff it into model context; (2) read/search/compare targets are not limited to git-tracked files. Plus three small real defects (SECURITY_CHECKS lookup throws on 'constructor'; buildFallbackPlan returns ok:true unvalidated; unsafe hunk id throws instead of ok:false), no cap on run probes, and three missing boundary tests. (1) changes delta's design record.

## Options
- **opt-a:** ship as-is; record (1), (2), run cap, TOCTOU as 675 requirements; decline the rest. Con: ships a plan schema whose compare probe can read arbitrary refs; DEC-0018 said mediums are not shipped open.
- **opt-b (recommended):** fix now: compare revisions restricted to the code-supplied merge-base SHA and HEAD only (intended semantics: RFC-0052's compare probe compares base against head and nothing else); Object.hasOwn lookup; fallback plan validated against the schema, fail-closed; unsafe hunk id -> ok:false; run-probe cap; the three boundary tests; validate.ts header reworded until (2) closes. (2) stays a HARD requirement on 675 (task text amended in #1162). Fresh three-reviewer round, then sign. Con: one more round on the critical path.

## Counter-argument
(1) is only exploitable by whoever authors the plan, which is the strong model under framework control, so one could call it theoretical. But plans are derived from untrusted diff content and the stash is shared across sessions; a confused-deputy path to .env is exactly what RFC-0043 exists to deny.

## Problem
657.3 (PR #1163, head ea8a2c6c, signed, all three approved) adds a doctor check and an execute-time sentinel for ignoring .ai-sdlc/artifacts. gitignoreCovers matches only the exact line, so `artifacts/`, `.ai-sdlc/` and `.ai-sdlc/*` are missed. The doctor check warns falsely on this repository (root .gitignore has `artifacts/`) and execute can append a redundant sentinel block. Push is held anyway on the lease-push question.

## Options

body:
## Problem
Round 3 review of AISDLC-667 (operator-dispatch loop skill, RFC-0051; executor epsilon, worktree .worktrees/aisdlc-667, nothing pushed): code and security reviewers both reject. The caller binding added after round 1 anchors trust on inputs the caller controls. An executor can create a scratch repo, forge hierarchy.json (its own claude pid as operator-dispatch) and agent-role.yaml, add a real worktree for another task, and run cli-hierarchy tick with --board-dir and --work-dir pointing at the scratch repo; every check passes and the push goes to the real origin with the operator's credentials. Second vector: trusted-root.ts runGit strips only GIT_DIR and GIT_WORK_TREE, so GIT_COMMON_DIR can redirect the root.

## Analysis
- Executors run Bash as the same OS user with the same git credentials. Any check performed by a CLI that the agent itself invokes can be satisfied by the agent. A same-user CLI check is therefore a guard against mistakes, not a security boundary. Same class as the self-asserted-anchor finding (AISDLC-590).
- The CLI adds no capability an executor lacks: it can already lease-push to ai-sdlc/<id> branches directly. Damage is bounded: main and master are unreachable and pushes are lease-only to task branches.
- The real boundary is a harness-level PreToolUse deny of tick, clear and route-decision for executor roles. That is AISDLC-684 (written, queued).

## Options
- opt-a: raise the bar (strip the full GIT_* set, require the CLI's own install location inside the verified main checkout), document as a mistake guard in the skill, docs and PR (DEC-0018 wording rule: no false security statements), close the test gaps.
- opt-b (taken): opt-a, plus state AISDLC-684 as a precondition for enabling tick with more than one executor.
- opt-c: drop the binding; rely on the 684 hook only.

## Counter-argument
opt-c is the most honest about where the boundary is and removes code that a reader may mistake for authentication. But the guard catches real accidents (an executor running tick from the wrong pane or checkout) at low cost, and opt-b's wording removes the risk of it being read as authentication. opt-a alone leaves multi-executor use enabled with no real boundary until 684 lands.

## Conditions on opt-b
- Reviewers judge the binding against the mistake-guard claim; the forged-roster path is disclosed in the PR body and docs as a known limit closed by 684, not counted as an open major.
- No sentence in the skill, docs or PR may call the binding authentication or authorization.
- 667 does not wait for 684 to merge; the precondition is on enabling multi-executor tick, not on landing the code.

rationale: A same-user CLI check cannot be a boundary; keep it as a labelled mistake guard and put the boundary in the 684 hook. Reversible; bounded damage (lease-only pushes to task branches).

body: Round 1 Opus security review of AISDLC-684 found the decision-mutation guard was a denylist (answer, resolve, override) that missed auto-expire, score-c with --store/--auto-apply, extend, and add with --autonomous-fallback plus --timebox followed by auto-expire, which lets an executor resolve its own escalation; and that 'no top-level task' was enforced only on the MCP create tools while Write/Edit/MultiEdit or the backlog CLI could still create one. Executors may run escalate, add without fallback or timebox, and read-only subcommands; everything else is refused, including subcommands added later. Editing an executor's own existing task file must keep working. Backlog.md's task_create schema has no id property and rejects unknown keys (published schema; server behaviour not tested). Counter-argument for opt-b: smaller change; but a denylist fails open on every new subcommand, and narrowing the guarantee leaves the scope-creep path open. Reversible.

rationale: Fail closed; resolving decisions belongs to planner and dispatch roles (DEC-0039).

summary: Default for the force-push governance setting when a repo sets nothing

options.description: Keep the stricter default; each adopter opts in to leaseOnOwnBranch
Default is leaseOnOwnBranch; stricter values are opt-in

body: Operator statement 2026-10-04: every project that adopts the framework runs into agents requesting authorization to lease-push their own branches; the default should be leaseOnOwnBranch. The framework requires rebasing task branches onto main, which needs a lease push, so the strict default blocks the required workflow and trains operators to approve prompts by reflex. Kept under the new default: plain force refused, protected branches refused, lease only on the agent's own branch. Current state: the allowForcePush setting defaults to never (STRICT_DEFAULTS in ai-sdlc-plugin/hooks/lib/governance-resolver.js, resolveForcePushMode) when a repo sets nothing; this repo's .ai-sdlc/agent-role.yaml sets leaseOnOwnBranch explicitly. Counter-argument: a permissive default lets an agent overwrite remote commits on its own branch that another session pushed; --force-with-lease refuses when the remote moved unexpectedly, which covers the common case. Reversible. Implemented by AISDLC-710.

rationale: Operator decision; the strict default blocks the framework's own rebase workflow in every adopter repo.
by: Dominique Legault (operator), recorded by planner (Claude Fable 5.1)

summary: Pre-push DoR gate blocks a rebased branch on an unrelated task file from main; how to unblock PR #1181 and later rebasers

options.description: Wait for the task file on main to be fixed before any rebased branch pushes
One-push skip of the DoR gate for the blocked branch, fix the task file on main, and file the gate fix
Standing permission to skip the DoR gate

body: The pre-push DoR gate (scripts/check-dor-gate.sh) evaluates remote-sha..local-sha. After a rebase and lease push the remote sha is the old pre-rebase head, so the range includes every commit main gained, and the gate evaluates task files the branch never touched. The AISDLC-705 task file on main fails Gate 5 (no affected surface named), so every rebasing branch is refused. The blocked branch's own diff is unchanged and passes; CI still evaluates the PR's own task changes. Counter-argument for opt-a: no skip variable is ever used; but it leaves every rebasing branch blocked on a docs merge cycle for a defect in the gate itself. opt-b conditions: only the DoR gate variable, only when the gate output names only the unrelated file, disclosed in the PR body; the standing rule against routine skip variables is unchanged. Also ruled in the same exchange: the CLAUDE.md Hooks item 8 text for AISDLC-694 goes in a docs-only follow-up PR right after its implementation PR merges, not into the already-approved PR and not parked for the operator. Also amends DEC-0045: the coordinated executor restart happens after the project-scoped session names task merges (instead of after 667 and 688), run from the planner side once dispatch reports all executors at a task boundary. Reversible.

rationale: Unblocks without losing a check; fixes the cause (AISDLC-712) and the instance (705 task body).

summary: Admission test for governance rules: necessity and velocity impact; no rule may block on human intervention

options.description: Keep adding guards case by case on reviewer findings
Every new or changed governance rule must pass an admission test; existing rules are audited against it

body: Operator statement 2026-10-04 (quote): "Going forward any new governance rules must go through scrutiny on why it's necessary and how it affects project velocity. Project velocity and throughput are of highest importance; if we have blockers that require human intervention then the project velocity drops to zero which is catastrophic for a project, never again can this type of governance rule drop velocity to zero." Trigger: the force-push setting defaulted to never (AISDLC-663), so agents in every adopting repository asked the operator to authorize lease pushes to their own branches, a step the framework's rebase workflow requires; the same week no agent could land a release PR and several sessions waited for the operator's direct word. Planner interpretation, made concrete by AISDLC-711. Admission test for any hook, gate, refusal, required check or governance default: (1) necessity: the concrete harm prevented, with an incident or a credible threat, and why existing controls do not cover it; (2) velocity impact: which documented workflows it touches and how often it fires on the happy path in a fresh adopter repository, which must be never; (3) exit: every refusal names an agent-resolvable next step (sanctioned command, config key and value, or escalation to another agent session); a rule whose only exit is a human is rejected, except legal, money, and accounts or credentials; (4) default: the documented workflow runs with nothing configured, stricter values are opt-in; (5) evidence after shipping: refusals are counted and the rule is reviewed, and removed or narrowed if it blocks more than it protects. Counter-argument: security reviewers will find real gaps whose simplest fix is a hard block, and this test slows or rejects those; accepted, because a block that stops all work or is approved by reflex protects nothing; the narrowest matcher, detect-and-report, or a sanctioned path is preferred. Reversible.

rationale: Operator decision. A guard whose only exit is the operator drops throughput to zero when he is away.
by: Dominique Legault (operator), recorded by planner (Claude Fable 5.1)

summary: AISDLC-702: must governance.releaseAuthors be configured, and who edits the governance config for this repository?

options.description: releaseAuthors is required; a repository without it refuses every release PR

Effective set is releaseAuthors, else mergeAuthors, else the release-please bot identities; refusal names the author login and the key; this repository's line is applied through a task on the operator's word
Default to the repository owner

body: The release source kind added by AISDLC-702 required releaseAuthors with no fallback, so with nothing configured the release path refuses, which conflicts with DEC-0048 (the documented workflow runs under default configuration). In this repository release PRs are authored by the personal access token owner, the same identity agents push as, so the author check does not distinguish a release PR from an agent PR; the controls are the exact release branch, the content allowlist, green required checks, the allowMerge kill switch and the hook-level role restriction, and the docs must say so (DEC-0038 wording rule). Switching release-please to the workflow token is rejected because pull requests created with it do not trigger CI. The dispatch session asked the planner to edit `.ai-sdlc/agent-role.yaml`, a path blocked for agent roles; the planner declined to make an edit another session was refused and took it to the operator, who answered: write it into a task so an executor applies it (AISDLC-714). The absence of any sanctioned path for agents to change governance config is added to the AISDLC-711 audit. Counter-argument for opt-a: failing closed is the safest default for a merge path; but it makes every adopter configure a key before their first release, and the refusal message now names the exact fix. Reversible.

rationale: Defaults must let the documented workflow run; the author check is not the control under a shared identity; config change routed through a task with the operator's direct word.

summary: Release path role restriction: disclosed limit or hook rule; and corrections to DEC-0049 and DEC-0050

options.description: Leave the CLI role check as a disclosed limit
File a narrow hook-level deny for executor sessions as its own task; correct the earlier records

body: The Opus reviewer of the release merge path suggested a hook-level deny of the release source kind for sessions holding an active task; the executor did not add it, citing DEC-0048. Applying the DEC-0048 admission test: necessity (release timing belongs to the planner, DEC-0042, and the CLI check is only a mistake guard, DEC-0038); velocity (never fires on the documented executor workflow); exit (escalate to the dispatch session); default (planner-run releases work unconfigured). It passes, so it is filed as its own task (717) and not added to the in-flight PRs. Corrections recorded here: (1) DEC-0050 listed 'the hook-level role restriction' among the release path's controls; no hook-level control exists yet; the correct term is the CLI role mistake guard. (2) DEC-0049's one-push skip of the DoR gate could not be executed, because the lease-push guard accepts only one exact command form with no environment prefix; the blocked branch waited for the task-file fix on main instead. Lesson recorded for the governance audit: a refusal must never suggest an exit that another guard forbids. (3) The 684 review loop has a stop rule: after round 2, a finding of the form 'another shell construction passes the pattern matcher' is a disclosed limit unless it is a false positive on normal work or needs no deliberate evasion. (4) The role-resolution consolidation (718) and the dogfood CLI resolution order (716) are filed as tasks. Counter-argument for opt-a: every new hook rule is one more thing that can refuse; accepted here because the matcher is narrow and the exit is another agent. Reversible.

rationale: Passes the DEC-0048 admission test; the hook is where the boundary belongs; earlier records corrected.

summary: Release merge path and the allowMerge master switch

options.description: Document that allowMerge does not govern release merges
Release merges are refused unless allowMerge is onGreenClean or governance.allowReleaseMerge is true; refusal names both keys
Honor allowMerge strictly

body: The backlog merge path refuses all agent-initiated merges under allowMerge never; the release path overrode it locally, which kept the round-1 security finding alive. A switch must mean what its name says. Letting agents merge is a grant of authority an operator opts into, so a default of false does not conflict with DEC-0048. This repository needs releaseAuthors and allowReleaseMerge, both applied through backlog task 714; the operator approved the second line directly. Reversible.

rationale: One master switch operators can reason about, with a narrow explicit grant for release PRs.

summary: Who may edit .ai-sdlc governance config

options.description: Keep the hardcoded floor: no agent session may edit anything under .ai-sdlc with Write or Edit
Internal sessions may edit config through reviewed pull requests when a task names the change; the block applies to untrusted runs, and CI blocks outside pull requests that touch config

body: Operator statement 2026-10-04 (quote): "I never asked for this, the only thing I asked for was that untrusted PRs from external sources like github PRs couldn't make modifications to the config of ai-sdlc, not internal trusted agents operating on my behalf. If I have to manually make changes to the config and commit and push and merge those changes then that dramatically affects developer velocity." Findings: the hook floor (added by AISDLC-567, kept absolute by AISDLC-599) refuses Write and Edit under .ai-sdlc for every session with no role or trust check; nine agent and command bodies say never edit; shell writes are not matched; no CI check stops an outside pull request from changing config. So the rule stops trusted sessions and not the untrusted source. Tradeoff recorded: internal agents can then change the rules that constrain agents, through reviewed pull requests; reviewers treat an unexplained loosening as a major finding and the digest lists every merged config change (see DEC-0053 for decisions that weaken controls). Implemented by backlog task 720. Reversible.

rationale: Operator decision: the config block was only ever meant for untrusted external pull requests.

summary: Review cost: two reviewers by default for low-risk PRs, and no opus security review for test-only and docs-adjacent changes

options.description: Keep three reviewers including an opus security review on every code PR

Two reviewers (combined correctness reviewer plus security) by default when a PR touches no trust-chain path; correctness reviewer only when the change is test-only or docs-adjacent; the full three-reviewer set stays for trust-chain paths

body: Operator direction 2026-10-04: prioritise velocity and token cost over governance; 126 tasks are open and recent trust-chain PRs took three review rounds each with an opus security review. The planner put two levers to the operator as decisions that loosen a review requirement and so need his explicit answer (DEC-0053); he answered: "approved on both cost levers, file them". Conditions written into the tasks: the reviewer set is derived from the diff by a deterministic classifier and re-derived by the CI verifier from the same diff, never taken from a field the signer writes; any trust-chain path in the diff forces the full set; a repository can opt back into three reviewers; the attestation records which set applied and why. Counter-argument: fewer independent reviews miss more defects, and security issues hide in ordinary code; mitigated by keeping security review on all non-trivial source changes, the full set on trust-chain paths, CodeQL on every PR, and a comparison window before the default flips. Interim until the staged review of RFC-0052 is live, which replaces fixed reviewer sets with risk-based planning. Reversible.

rationale: Operator decision: approved on both cost levers.

summary: Governance friction audit: which existing controls are deleted, kept or changed

options.description: Keep the existing controls and repair them one defect at a time
Apply the audit decisions row by row as decided with the operator

body:
On 2026-10-04 the planner audited the existing governance controls (catalogue of hooks, git hooks, CI checks, review and attestation rules; cycle metrics for 45 merged PRs; 182 hook refusals over five days; token ledger) and the operator decided each row through the decision rubric, in the order question the requirement, delete, simplify, accelerate, automate.

Row 1: the duplicate CI workflow stops running on pull requests and keeps running on pushes to main; any job unique to it moves into the gate first.

Row 2: the pre-push coverage gate and the Stop-hook coverage run are deleted; CI remains the coverage gate; the developer agent's instructions state a coverage requirement above the CI floor so agents overshoot.

Row 3: the pre-push readiness gate and the commit-time and push-time backlog-drift checks are deleted and the CI readiness check joins the required rollup.

Row 4: the push-time attestation verify stays and nothing is deleted there; the CI attestation poll is to be sized later.

Row 5: the workflow that rebases every open pull request after each merge is deleted; branches are rebased only on conflict; the up-to-date requirement was already off; skew is caught by the main health monitor.

Row 6: the merge ban stays because it is the only guard against an agent merging an outside contributor's green pull request; its matcher is fixed to apply only when the merge command is the one being run.

Row 7: the session scratch directory and OS temp directories become writable by default; worktree confinement stays otherwise.

Row 8: prompt rules live in one source and appear once per agent prompt as one line naming the sanctioned alternative.

Row 9: incremental review is treated as a defect: it fired only after an approval and only on one path; it must work after a rejection, on every review path, with the reviewer's prior findings, and report how often it fires; the interim rule of two rounds then a planner ruling stays until delta rounds are real.

Coverage floors: 90 percent lines for packages at 93 percent or above, 85 percent for dogfood, dashboard and the conformance runner, patch coverage 90 percent; the developer agent's stated requirement is 95 percent.

Counter-argument recorded for the deletions: failures move from seconds locally to minutes in CI; accepted because the local gates were slow, duplicated CI and were a top source of repair work. Reversible.

rationale: Operator decisions row by row on 2026-10-04 and 2026-10-05.
by: Dominique Legault (operator), recorded by planner (Claude Fable 5.1)
